porbos.title: When Even the Tribe Could No Longer Protect • Hijrah Is Not Fleeing • Why Abyssinia • The First Caravan

blocks.0: When Even the Tribe Could No Longer Protect
blocks.1: In the last dars we saw what came down upon those who had no tribe behind them. Scorching sand, a rock on the chest, a spear, burning coals. One question was left hanging there. Were those who had a tribe safe!
blocks.2: The answer is, no. Hands were laid on them with measure, because if a hand was laid on one, the tribe would demand an accounting of blood. But the pressure still came. Only its face was different. Today we shall hear of those people who had lineage, a house, a name; yet they too had to pay the price of the din.
blocks.4: He was an honoured man of Banu Taym, a well-known merchant of Makkah, one who had the genealogies of the Quraysh by heart. The people of Makkah loved him, sat in his gatherings. A few years after accepting Islam, one day he said to the Prophet {{1}}, must we stay hidden! With the permission of the Prophet {{2}} he stood in al-Masjid al-Haram, and openly called people to Allah and His Messenger.
blocks.5: This was the first public speech in the history of Islam. The Quraysh pounced. ‘Utbah ibn Rabi‘ah came forward and began striking him in the face with a shoe. With the heel of the shoe he crushed his nose and mouth, the face filled with blood, he could not be recognised.
blocks.6: Banu Taym came and wrapped him in a cloth and carried him home. Everyone took it that he would not survive. All day he lay unconscious. In the evening he came to. What were his first words when he opened his mouth! How is the Prophet {{1}}.
blocks.7: His mother wanted to feed him. He would not eat. He said, first tell me, how is the Prophet {{1}}. Until I see him well with my own eyes, I will put nothing in my mouth.
blocks.8: In the darkness of night his mother took him, supporting him, to the Prophet {{1}}. Only after seeing him well did Abu Bakr (RA) put anything in his mouth.{{2}}
blocks.9: Not once did he ask about the state of his own broken face.
blocks.11: Talhah (RA) too was a man of Banu Taym, a young merchant. In the course of trade he had gone to Sham; there he heard from a monk that the time had come for a prophet to appear in Arabia. Returning to Makkah he inquired, and accepted Islam.
blocks.12: Nawfal ibn Khuwaylid was a fierce man of the Quraysh; the people of Makkah called him ‘the Lion of the Quraysh’. He brought a rope and tied Talhah and Abu Bakr (RA) together, and left them lying in the sun. Banu Taym did not come to free them.
blocks.13: The people of Makkah from then on called the two ‘al-Qarinayn’; the two bound together. Two men of an honoured lineage, tied with one rope, lying in the sun; and their tribe looking away.{{1}}
blocks.15: ‘Uthman ibn ‘Affan (RA) was a man of Banu Umayyah, wealthy and shy by nature. His uncle al-Hakam ibn Abi al-‘As would tie him tightly and say, you have left the religion of your fathers and grandfathers for a new religion! Until you return, this bond will not be loosed. ‘Uthman (RA) would say, I will never give it up.
blocks.16: Al-Zubayr ibn al-‘Awwam (RA) was then a mere boy. His uncle would wrap him in a mat, light a fire beneath and smoke him, and say, return to disbelief. The little al-Zubayr would say from inside the smoke, no, I will never return to disbelief.{{1}}
blocks.18: Mus‘ab (RA) was the best-dressed young man of Makkah. His mother Khunas bint Malik had raised him in pampering and luxury. His clothes, his shoes, his perfume; the young men of Makkah talked about these.
blocks.19: He used to go secretly to Dar al-Arqam. One day someone saw, and it reached his mother’s ears. His mother shut him up in the house. Cut down his food and clothing. In the end Mus‘ab (RA) slipped away and went to Abyssinia.
blocks.20: That perfumed young man of Makkah later wore a cloak so torn and patched that the Companions’ eyes filled with tears on seeing it. A man who had everything gave up everything for the din.{{1}}
blocks.22: Khalid (RA) was one of the early Muslims; it is said, number four or five. His father Abu Uhayhah was an influential leader of Makkah. Getting the news, the father beat him with a stick so hard that the stick broke. Then on a hot day he shut him up, cutting off food and water, saying, burn to death in the sun.
blocks.23: Khalid (RA) told his father, by Allah, he is a true prophet; I will follow him. In the end he too migrated to Abyssinia.{{1}}
blocks.25: ‘Uthman ibn Maz‘un (RA) was one of the early Muslims, a man of restrained nature. On returning from Abyssinia he entered Makkah under the protection of al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. But he did not feel right. He thought, my brothers are being beaten in the way of Allah, and I am going about safely under the protection of a polytheist; this is not right.
blocks.26: He went to al-Walid and openly returned his protection. Some days later he was sitting in an assembly of the Quraysh. A poet was reciting; ‘Uthman (RA) objected to one of his remarks. A man of the Quraysh came up and punched him in the eye so hard that the eye swelled and turned blue.
blocks.27: Al-Walid, sitting nearby, said, nephew, if you had stayed under my protection your eye would have been saved. ‘Uthman (RA) said, no. My good eye, rather, needed what happened to this one, in the way of Allah. I am now under the protection of One far mightier than you.{{1}}
blocks.29: ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab’s sister Fatimah bint al-Khattab and her husband Sa‘id ibn Zayd (RA) had accepted Islam in secret. ‘Umar was then a fierce enemy of Islam. Getting the news, he beat his own sister; blood came to her mouth.
blocks.30: That beating is what in the end stopped ‘Umar; that comes later in today’s dars itself.
blocks.31: Now the Picture in One Place
blocks.32: On one side, sand on the backs of slaves. On the other, ropes, mats, smoke, a broken stick, imprisonment at the hands of a mother, hunger at the hands of a father, on sons of honoured houses. The kind of persecution was different. But no one was spared.
blocks.33: The tribe could only hold back open killing. All the rest still happened; and often that blow came from inside the house itself, from a father’s hand, an uncle’s hand, a mother’s hand.
blocks.34: Holding on to the din in Makkah was becoming impossible day by day. Even today the thing fits in one place. When someone with a strong tribe wants to hold to the din, he is told, ‘you have drowned the family’s honour’. And the one who has no one is simply thrown out of the job.
blocks.35: The face of the pressure changes. The pressure remains. And the hardest pressure often comes from no outsider; it comes from the people of the house. From exactly this place today’s dars begins.
blocks.37: When the persecution went beyond endurance, the Prophet {{1}} showed a way. He told the Companions, it would be good if you went out toward Abyssinia. There is a king there in whose court no one is wronged.{{2}}
blocks.38: It sounds easy. Inside it is a hard decision. Leaving home. The soil of birth, parents, relatives, business, familiar roads; leaving it all behind to go to an unfamiliar land, where the language is different, the religion different.
blocks.39: A thought comes to many minds. Does hijrah mean retreating in defeat! The Qur’an says the opposite. It came down from the heavens
blocks.41: Say, O My servants who believe, fear your Lord. For those who do good deeds in this world there is good. And Allah’s earth is spacious. Surely the patient will be given their reward without reckoning.{{1}}
blocks.42: Allah’s earth is spacious. To move away from where one cannot call upon Allah to a place where one can; this is not fleeing. This is a strategy for saving the din.
blocks.43: The Prophet {{1}} later said, the true muhajir is the one who gives up the things Allah has forbidden.{{2}}
blocks.44: That is, the real point of hijrah is not changing place. It is leaving behind. Even today the point is useful. An environment where, if you stand in it, prayer is missed, the eyes cannot be controlled, faith slowly erodes; moving away from that environment is also a kind of hijrah.
blocks.45: A workplace, a gathering of friends, a world sunk into the phone; whatever pulls you down a little more every day. Giving that up is called hijrah. And that giving up is never a defeat.
blocks.47: The question is natural. There were other countries. Yemen was near, Sham a familiar trade route. Why Abyssinia. Abyssinia was then a Christian kingdom, across the Red Sea; the region of today’s Ethiopia. The king’s title was al-Najashi; his real name Ashamah.
blocks.48: There were several reasons. One, Abyssinia was beyond the reach of the Quraysh. The sea in between. The Quraysh could not simply go there and make trouble. Two, Abyssinia had an old trade relationship with Makkah. Arab merchants went back and forth regularly, so the country was not entirely unfamiliar.
blocks.49: Three, and this is the real reason; the reputation of al-Najashi. About him on the lips of Arab merchants there was one thing only; no one suffers injustice in his court. The Prophet {{1}} did not send the Companions to an enemy country. He sent them to a ruler who, though of another religion, was a man of justice.
blocks.50: There is something to learn here. With one who does justice, a relationship of refuge can be kept; even if he is of another religion. And from one who does wrong, one must move away; even if he is a man of one’s own tribe.
blocks.51: The yardstick is not the name of a religion. The yardstick is justice. There is something else. The Prophet {{1}} did not leave the weak Companions to fate. He fixed a goal, inquired where it was safe, chose the name of a king, and then sent the group.
blocks.52: Tawakkul does not mean sitting with folded hands. It means making arrangements, using intelligence, then leaving the result in Allah’s hands. One who says, Allah is my reliance, nothing needs to be done; he has not understood tawakkul. The Prophet {{1}} placed his trust in Allah, and did the work with flawless planning.
blocks.54: The fifth year of prophethood, the month of Rajab. In the darkness of night a group of people quietly left Makkah. About twelve men, four or five women. They walked toward the port of Shu‘aybah; hiding by day, moving by night.
blocks.55: In this group were ‘Uthman ibn ‘Affan (RA), and his wife Ruqayyah; the daughter of the Prophet {{1}}. There were Abu Hudhayfah ibn ‘Utbah, and ‘Uthman ibn Maz‘un (RA) and a few others.
blocks.56: The Prophet {{1}} later said of ‘Uthman and Ruqayyah (RA), after Ibrahim and Lut, these are the first who migrated with their family in the way of Allah.{{2}}
blocks.57: The Quraysh found out and followed, as far as the seashore. Arriving, they saw that a trading ship had just left the quay. The Muslims had boarded and hoisted sail. The Quraysh had to return empty-handed.
blocks.58: Some call getting a boat at just the right time a coincidence. Reading the Sirah one understands that the One who gave the order of hijrah had also kept the boat at the quay. Arriving in Abyssinia they got, for the first time, something they had not had in Makkah for many years. A full prayer, under the open sky, without fear.
blocks.59: The thing we get every day and do not notice; prostration without fear. For that thing a group of people had to leave their country.

footnotes.0: The first public speech of Abu Bakr (RA) in al-Masjid al-Haram, the beating with a shoe at the hands of ‘Utbah ibn Rabi‘ah, Banu Taym carrying him off unconscious, and the account of asking on regaining consciousness ‘how is the Prophet {{1}}’ and eating nothing without seeing him: Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham. The narration is of the Sirah works; the chain is mursal. But Abu Bakr’s (RA) open da‘wah and his being persecuted for it is well known in the Sirah and hadith works.
footnotes.1: Concerning Talhah (RA) hearing from a monk in Sham of the coming of a prophet, and Nawfal ibn Khuwaylid tying Talhah and Abu Bakr (RA) together and the name ‘al-Qarinayn’: Ibn Ishaq; Ibn al-Athir, Usd al-Ghabah. The narration is of the Sirah and Tabaqat works; the chain is mursal.
footnotes.2: The tying of ‘Uthman (RA) by his uncle al-Hakam ibn Abi al-‘As, and the torture of al-Zubayr (RA) by his uncle by wrapping him in a mat and smoking him: Ibn Sa‘d, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra; Ibn al-Athir, Usd al-Ghabah. The narration is of the Tabaqat and history works; the chain is mursal.
footnotes.3: Concerning the luxurious life of Mus‘ab ibn ‘Umayr (RA), his imprisonment at the hands of his mother Khunas bint Malik, the hijrah to Abyssinia and later poverty: Ibn Sa‘d, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra; Ibn Ishaq. The narration is of the Sirah and Tabaqat works; the chain is mursal. The incident of the Companions weeping on seeing his torn cloak comes in Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 1276 and 4047 (in connection with Uhud).
footnotes.4: Concerning the early acceptance of Islam by Khalid ibn Sa‘id ibn al-‘As (RA), the beating by his father Abu Uhayhah, imprisonment with hunger, and the hijrah to Abyssinia: Ibn Ishaq; Ibn Sa‘d, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra. The narration is of the Sirah and Tabaqat works; the chain is mursal.
footnotes.5: Concerning ‘Uthman ibn Maz‘un (RA) taking the protection of al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, returning it openly, and being struck in the eye in the assembly of poetry and his reply: Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham. The narration is of the Sirah works; the chain is mursal.
footnotes.6: Concerning the advice of the Prophet {{1}} to migrate to Abyssinia and the statement ‘there is a king there in whose court no one is wronged’: Ibn Ishaq; Musnad Ahmad, hadith 1740 (via Umm Salamah (RA), part of the long narration of Ja‘far (RA)). Many hadith scholars have called the narration hasan.
footnotes.8: ‘Al-muhajiru man hajara ma naha Llahu ‘anhu’; the true muhajir is the one who abandons what Allah has forbidden. Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 10; via ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr (RA). ✓ Verified.
footnotes.9: Concerning the number of participants in the first hijrah (about twelve men and four or five women) and the hijrah of ‘Uthman and Ruqayyah (RA): Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham, chapter on Abyssinia; Ibn Sa‘d. There is variation in the reports about the number and some of the names. The statement of the Prophet {{1}} about ‘Uthman (RA), ‘the first family to migrate after Ibrahim and Lut’, is the narration of Ibn Ishaq; this part is mursal.

quiz.q: Who gave the first public speech in the history of Islam?
o: Abu Bakr (RA)
Hamzah ibn ‘Abd al-Muttalib (RA)
‘Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA)
Ja‘far ibn Abi Talib (RA)
quiz.e: Abu Bakr (RA) called openly in al-Masjid al-Haram; that very day ‘Utbah ibn Rabi‘ah struck him with a shoe.

quiz.q: Regaining consciousness after the beating, what were Abu Bakr’s (RA) first words?
o: Is my face entirely all right
How is the Prophet ﷺ
Where is ‘Utbah ibn Rabi‘ah now
Give me a sip of water
quiz.e: He put nothing even in his mouth until he saw the Prophet ﷺ well with his own eyes.

quiz.q: Which two, whom Nawfal bound with one rope, were called ‘al-Qarinayn’?
o: Hamzah and ‘Umar (RA)
‘Uthman and al-Zubayr (RA)
Abu Bakr and Talhah (RA)
Ja‘far and ‘Ali (RA)
quiz.e: Nawfal would tie Talhah and Abu Bakr (RA) of Banu Taym with one rope and leave them in the sun.

quiz.q: What persecution did the uncles inflict on ‘Uthman and al-Zubayr (RA)?
o: Laying them on scorching sand
Making them wear iron armour in the sun
Placing a heavy rock on the chest
Wrapping in a mat and smoking
quiz.e: ‘Uthman (RA) was tied up by his uncle al-Hakam; al-Zubayr (RA) was wrapped in a mat with a fire lit beneath and smoked.

quiz.q: Who shut Mus‘ab ibn ‘Umayr (RA) in the house after Islam?
o: His mother Khunas bint Malik
His uncle and the elders of the tribe
Abu Jahl and his companions
Umayyah ibn Khalaf and his men
quiz.e: The mother shut up the best-dressed young man of Makkah, stopped his food and clothing; in the end he slipped away to Abyssinia.

quiz.q: What punishment did the father of Khalid ibn Sa‘id (RA) give him?
o: Only threw him out of the house
Beat him with a stick and shut him up with hunger
Only deprived him of inheritance
Only forced him to leave Makkah
quiz.e: The father beat him until the stick broke, then on a hot day shut him up, cutting off food and water.

quiz.q: Who says, ‘my good eye too needed this, in the way of Allah’?
o: ‘Ammar ibn Yasir (RA)
Khabbab ibn al-Aratt (RA)
‘Uthman ibn Maz‘un (RA)
Khalid ibn Sa‘id (RA)
quiz.e: After returning the protection of al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, ‘Uthman ibn Maz‘un (RA) was punched in the eye in the assembly of poetry.

quiz.q: How did the persecution of Companions with tribes differ from that of slaves?
o: They were not persecuted at all
They were only fined
The pressure was measured; imprisonment, rope, smoke
They were only expelled from their country
quiz.e: The tribe held back open killing; all the rest happened, and the blow often came from inside the house.

quiz.q: What is the core message of the introductory passage?
o: With a tribe there is no hardship
Slaves alone were the most persecuted
Persecution was then only in the city of Makkah
Everyone had to pay the price of the din
quiz.e: Even one who had lineage and name had to bear ropes, smoke and imprisonment; the kind was different.

quiz.q: What does the dars say if the wrongdoer one should move away from is one’s own relative?
o: Stay for the sake of kinship
Move away from the wrong even if he is one’s own
Bear everything in silence
Take open revenge when the chance comes
quiz.e: The yardstick is justice; at the start we saw that the hardest blow often comes at the hand of the people of the house.

quiz.q: What can be learned from the Companions of the introduction when the people of the house obstruct holding to the din?
o: Cutting off the relationship completely
Giving up the din quietly to avoid trouble
Raising great discord at home
Not giving up the din, moving to a safe place if necessary
quiz.e: Mus‘ab, Khalid, ‘Uthman ibn Maz‘un (RA) bore the pressure of home, moved to Abyssinia when needed, and did not give up the din.

quiz.q: What comes regarding hijrah in verse 10 of Surah al-Zumar?
o: Makkah is the best city in the world
The patient have no reward
Hijrah is only the work of the weak
Allah’s earth is spacious
quiz.e: ‘Wa ardu Llahi wasi‘ah’; to move away from where Allah cannot be called upon is not fleeing.

quiz.q: Who is the true muhajir in the words of the Prophet ﷺ?
o: One who gives up what Allah has forbidden
One who goes from Makkah to Madinah
One who crosses the sea toward Abyssinia
One who leaves tribe and lineage
quiz.e: ‘Al-muhajiru man hajara ma naha Llahu ‘anhu’; Sahih al-Bukhari 10. Not change of place; giving up the forbidden is the essence.

quiz.q: ‘Hijrah is not fleeing’; what is the core argument?
o: Moving away to protect faith is a strategy
Fleeing is not permissible in any situation
Hijrah is only preparation for an impending war
Worship is not possible anywhere but Makkah
quiz.e: Surah al-Zumar 10 says Allah’s earth is spacious; moving away from where Allah cannot be called upon is not weakness.

quiz.q: What form of ‘hijrah’ in today’s context does the dars mention?
o: Changing one’s whole country altogether
Leaving any job whatever
Leaving the environment that erodes faith
Leaving the city for a village
quiz.e: Leaving the company or world that pulls you down every day is also hijrah; the true muhajir leaves the forbidden.

quiz.q: Why did the Prophet ﷺ choose Abyssinia for refuge chiefly?
o: A Muslim ruler was there
The king there was a man of justice
It was the nearest from Makkah
Arabic language and custom prevailed there
quiz.e: Though al-Najashi was a Christian, no one suffered injustice in his court; besides, the sea as a barrier and old trade ties.

quiz.q: What principle comes from sending the Companions to the Christian al-Najashi?
o: No relations with anyone of another religion
The yardstick of refuge is justice, not the name of a religion
One may go only to a Muslim ruler
Going to any king makes that refuge safe
quiz.e: One who does justice can be taken as refuge, even if of another religion; from one who does wrong one must move away.

quiz.q: What is the proof, in the hijrah to Abyssinia, that ‘tawakkul does not mean sitting’?
o: The Companions merely sat making du‘a
No one made any preparation for it
The Prophet ﷺ planned and chose the destination and sent them
Al-Najashi himself had invited them beforehand
quiz.e: Making arrangements, using intelligence, then leaving the result in Allah’s hands; this is tawakkul.

quiz.q: In deciding on refuge or relationship with anyone, what is the yardstick?
o: Exactly which religion he belongs to
How influential and powerful he is
Whether he is a close relative
Whether he does justice
quiz.e: The Prophet ﷺ chose the Christian al-Najashi for his justice; one must move away from the oppressor.

quiz.q: Which daughter and son-in-law of the Prophet ﷺ were in the first caravan of hijrah?
o: Fatimah and ‘Ali (RA)
Zaynab and Abu al-‘As ibn al-Rabi‘
Umm Kulthum and ‘Uthman (RA)
Ruqayyah and ‘Uthman (RA)
quiz.e: The Prophet ﷺ said, after Ibrahim and Lut, these are the first to migrate with their family.

quiz.q: On what did the Companions of the first caravan escape at the seashore?
o: Boarding a trading ship
Hiding in a mountain cave
A ship sent by al-Najashi
Swimming across all night
quiz.e: The Quraysh followed and arrived to find the ship had just left the quay; they had to return empty-handed.

porbos.title: Returning on False News • The Second Hijrah • The Quraysh Envoys in the Court of al-Najashi • The Speech of Ja‘far (RA) • The Recitation That Wet the Beard • The Trap of the Second Day • The Absentee Funeral Prayer for al-Najashi • A Speech of One Sitting That Remained • Moving to a Safe Place Is Not Shame

blocks.1: A few months later news reached Abyssinia that the situation in Makkah had changed; the Quraysh had supposedly softened, or many had supposedly become Muslim. The news was false. On this news some Companions returned home. Coming near Makkah they realised that nothing had changed; indeed it was harder than before.
blocks.2: This time there was no way in. One whose tribe was strong perhaps slipped in. The rest had to enter by taking someone’s protection. ‘Uthman ibn Maz‘un (RA) had entered Makkah under the protection of al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah; later he himself returned that protection, saying, Allah’s protection is enough for me.{{1}}
blocks.3: From here is something worth remembering. In their haste to come out of hardship, people often believe news without verifying. What the heart wants to hear, the ear takes to be true.
blocks.4: Sitting inside a hardship, any news of relief tastes sweet. The patience to verify is not there then. Even today we do the same. The news that is pleasant to hear we believe without verifying, and even spread it. And what we do not like, we doubt even when there is proof.
blocks.5: The Companions, returning, saw that the news of relief had been imagination. One false report, and a whole caravan again facing persecution.
blocks.7: This time the Prophet {{1}} again gave permission for hijrah. This time the group was much bigger. About eighty-three men, and some eighteen women.{{2}}
blocks.8: In this group were Abu Salamah and Umm Salamah (RA), ‘Uthman ibn Maz‘un, al-Zubayr ibn al-‘Awwam (RA) and many well-known faces of Makkah. The leader of the group was Ja‘far ibn Abi Talib (RA). He was the cousin of the Prophet {{1}}, the elder brother of ‘Ali (RA). In face and nature he resembled the Prophet {{2}}.
blocks.9: The first time a small group had gone, quietly. This time about a hundred went. A large part of the Muslim community of Makkah. The Quraysh now understood that running to the seashore was no use. The Muslims were getting there.
blocks.10: So they changed tactics. Instead of running after the Muslims, they decided to strike straight at the court of al-Najashi. To make a refuge unsafe, there is no need to chase the refugee. It is enough to poison the mind of the one giving refuge.
blocks.11: This is exactly what the Quraysh set out to do. And from there one of the most beautiful scenes of the Sirah came about.
blocks.12: The Quraysh Envoys in the Court of al-Najashi
blocks.13: The Quraysh chose two shrewd men. ‘Amr ibn al-‘As and ‘Abdullah ibn Abi Rabi‘ah. Both eloquent, skilled in diplomacy. They sent with them things Abyssinia liked; fine leather, in plenty.
blocks.14: The plan was laid out. First, gifts were pressed into the hands of the great monks and courtiers of the court. Then they were told, when the king raises the matter, you will speak on our side.{{1}}
blocks.15: All arranged, the envoys stood before the king. They said, O king, some foolish youths of ours have abandoned the religion of their fathers and grandfathers. They have not entered your religion either. They have made up a new religion, which none of us knows, nor do you. They have come to your country and are hiding. Send them back; the elders of their tribes have sent you that request.
blocks.16: The monks of the court chimed in from the side, true, it is best to send them back. Al-Najashi did not agree. He said, no. Those who have taken refuge in my country, I will not hand them over to anyone before hearing them. Call them.
blocks.18: The Muslims came to the court. The king, beside him the monks, open books in their hands. Standing in front, a group of refugees whose fate now hung on the answer to one question. It was Ja‘far (RA) who spoke.
blocks.19: He gave no long preface. He began straight away with this; what we were, and what we became. He said, O king, we were an ignorant people. We worshipped idols. We ate carrion. We did evil deeds. We violated the rights of kin, we behaved badly to neighbours. Among us the strong devoured the weak.
blocks.20: Then Allah sent a messenger from among us. His lineage we know, his truthfulness we know, his purity we know. He called us to the One Allah. He said, give up idols. Speak the truth. Keep trusts. Give kin their due. Behave well to neighbours. Stop bloodshed. Do not eat the property of the orphan. Do not slander chaste women.
blocks.21: He taught us prayer, taught us zakah, taught us fasting. We believed him. For this very reason our people became our enemies. They persecuted us, so that we would go back to idols.
blocks.22: When we could bear no more, we came to your country. We chose you. We hope that with you we shall not be victims of injustice.{{1}}
blocks.23: The whole court was silent. He had drawn the whole picture of a people in a few sentences; where it was, and where the call of the One Allah took it.
blocks.24: The Recitation That Wet the Beard
blocks.25: Al-Najashi said, can you recite to me something of what Allah has sent down to your Prophet. Ja‘far (RA) began reciting from the beginning of Surah Maryam.
blocks.26: The story of Maryam and ‘Isa (peace be upon them). A story familiar to the ear of this Christian king, yet one he had never heard in so clear a tone.
blocks.28: And relate in this Book the account of Maryam, when she moved away from her family people to a place in the east. Then she drew a screen to hide herself from them. Then I sent My spirit to her, and he appeared before her in the form of a perfect human.{{1}}
blocks.30: Al-Najashi wept. Weeping, his beard became wet. The monks sitting beside him also wept, the pages of their books also became wet. Al-Najashi said, this word and what ‘Isa brought are as if the light of one lamp.
blocks.31: Then turning to the Quraysh envoys he said, go. By Allah, I will not hand them over to you. At the start of the day the decision had been that the Muslims would be sent back. One recitation, and the decision was overturned.
blocks.32: Diplomacy, gifts, bribes; all were in the envoys’ hands. In the Muslims’ hands there were only a few verses. It was the verses that won.
blocks.33: The Trap of the Second Day
blocks.34: ‘Amr ibn al-‘As was not one to give up easily. The next day he went to the court again. He said, O king, ask them one thing. What do they say about ‘Isa ibn Maryam.
blocks.35: The move was subtle. If the Muslims say ‘Isa is the son of Allah, they would go against their own Qur’an. And if they say he is only a servant, the Christian king will be angry.
blocks.36: A trap on both sides. The Muslims consulted among themselves. They decided, whatever Allah has said, we will say that; let the consequence be what it may. The king asked. Ja‘far (RA) said, our Prophet says of him, he is the servant of Allah and His Messenger, His spirit, and His word, which He cast to the virgin Maryam.{{1}}
blocks.37: Al-Najashi picked up a twig from the ground. He said, ‘Isa ibn Maryam was not even this much more than what you have said. Then he said to the Muslims, you are safe in my country. Whoever abuses you shall be punished.
blocks.38: He returned the Quraysh’s gifts. The envoys went back to Makkah empty-handed. There was fear in telling the truth. Telling it might finish everything. Yet they told it. And that very truth saved them.
blocks.39: The Absentee Funeral Prayer for al-Najashi
blocks.40: The envoys of the Quraysh returned empty-handed. But the story does not end here. A few years later al-Najashi accepted Islam. But in secret; had he announced it his throne would not have lasted, there would have been rebellion in the country.
blocks.41: Before the eyes of the Companions who had taken refuge in his country the matter went this far; the king who gave refuge himself accepted the din of those given refuge. The day he died, the Prophet {{1}} was in Madinah. A thousand miles away.
blocks.42: That very day the Prophet {{1}} told the Companions, today a righteous brother of yours has died; Ashamah. Then he took everyone to the praying ground. Formed rows. For the man whose body was in Abyssinia, not before their eyes, he led the funeral prayer; with four takbirs.{{2}}
blocks.43: A Christian king. Who had never seen the Prophet {{1}} with his eyes, nor set foot on the soil of Arabia. One justice, and the weeping of one recitation; these two things in the end brought him as far as faith.
blocks.44: That speech of one sitting by Ja‘far (RA) then did not only save one group. It opened a window for a whole country toward the din, and brought the king of that country up on to the path of Paradise.
blocks.45: The group that had been driven out of Makkah as weak brought a country’s king into the din. Who is weak and who is strong, that reckoning is different in Allah’s ledger.
blocks.46: A Speech of One Sitting That Remained
blocks.47: Two more things about that speech of Ja‘far (RA). First, what he did not say. He made no long complaint against the Quraysh. He did not weep and wail. He did not beg the king’s mercy.
blocks.48: He only laid out the truth in order; what we were, and what this din came and gave. That ordered truth stopped a whole court. Second, what the speech left behind.
blocks.49: Abyssinia remained a safe haven for the Muslims for many years afterward. Some returned from there long after the hijrah to Madinah; at the time of the conquest of Khaybar. When Ja‘far (RA) came back, the Prophet {{1}} said, I do not know in which I am happier; the conquest of Khaybar, or the coming of Ja‘far.{{2}}
blocks.50: One speech. Of one sitting. But when ordered true words are spoken in the right place, they work year after year. For many of us the opportunity comes; someone asks about the din, comes to argue, or simply wants to know.
blocks.51: If at that moment one has in hand an ordered answer like Ja‘far’s, a word of one sitting can travel very far. And if not, the opportunity slips away.
blocks.52: Moving to a Safe Place Is Not Shame
blocks.53: One thing from this whole episode of Abyssinia for today. Sometimes one has to change place to save the din. A city where, if you live in it, the children do not learn prayer, but learn the opposite. A job in which there is no way but the haram. A house or neighbourhood where every day a tug is felt on faith. A gathering of friends without leaving which your own prayer cannot survive.
blocks.54: Moving away from there is not weakness. The Companions loved Makkah. The Ka‘bah was there, the homeland was there, the graves of fathers and grandfathers were there. Yet by Allah’s command they moved away, because the din is bigger than soil.
blocks.55: But two things must be kept in mind. One, before moving, to settle on a safe destination. As the Prophet {{1}} chose Abyssinia first and made inquiries; he did not set out all of a sudden.
blocks.56: Two, on going to the new place, to take the din along with you; not to leave it behind. Many go from a bad environment to a good one, but take the inner habit along. Then even changing place is of no benefit.
blocks.57: The Companions did not get lost on going to Abyssinia. There too they remained Muslims, prayed together, held the din among themselves, and in the end carried the Qur’an as far as a royal court. Changing place helps only when a person takes the thing inside himself along with him.

footnotes.0: Ibn Ishaq narrates that a false report of the kind ‘the Quraysh have inclined toward Islam’ reached them as the reason why some of the first emigrants returned to Makkah; this part is mursal. The incident of ‘Uthman ibn Maz‘un (RA) taking the protection of al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah and later returning it is also narrated through Ibn Ishaq; mursal. The story of the ‘Gharaniq’, the recitation of verses praising idols, which has been tangled up in this context, is invalid both in chain and in substance; the verifying scholars have rejected it.
footnotes.1: Concerning the number of participants in the second hijrah (about eighty-three men, if Umm Salamah (RA) is counted; and about eighteen women): Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham. There is slight variation in the reports on the number.
footnotes.2: Concerning the Quraysh sending ‘Amr ibn al-‘As and ‘Abdullah ibn Abi Rabi‘ah to the court of al-Najashi with gifts of leather, and first winning over the courtiers with gifts: Ibn Ishaq; Musnad Ahmad, hadith 1740 (via Umm Salamah (RA)). Many have called the narration hasan.
footnotes.3: This speech of Ja‘far ibn Abi Talib (RA) in the court of al-Najashi is narrated at length in Musnad Ahmad, hadith 1740, via Umm Salamah (RA); it also comes through Ibn Ishaq in Sirah Ibn Hisham. Many hadith scholars have called the narration hasan. The dars presents the gist of the speech; the words are not verbatim.
footnotes.5: Concerning al-Najashi’s request to hear the Qur’an and Ja‘far’s (RA) recitation of Surah Maryam: Musnad Ahmad, hadith 1740 (via Umm Salamah (RA)); Ibn Ishaq. Exactly which part of the surah Ja‘far (RA) recited is not specified in the narration; the narration has ‘Surah Kaf-Ha-Ya-‘Ayn-Sad’, that is, the beginning of Surah Maryam.
footnotes.6: Concerning ‘Amr ibn al-‘As raising the question about ‘Isa (peace be upon him) on the second day and Ja‘far’s (RA) answer: Ibn Ishaq; Musnad Ahmad, hadith 1740. Many have called the narration hasan. The statement of the answer is consistent with Surah al-Nisa’ 171 and Surah Maryam 30–34.
footnotes.7: Concerning the news of the death of al-Najashi Ashamah reaching the Prophet {{1}}, his announcement ‘today a righteous brother of yours has died’, and leading the absentee funeral prayer: Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 1320, 1327 and 3877; Sahih Muslim, hadith 951; via Jabir and Abu Hurayrah (RA). The account of taking them to the praying ground, forming rows and leading the funeral prayer with four takbirs comes in Sunan Abi Dawud, hadith 3204. ✓ Verified.
footnotes.8: Concerning the statement of the Prophet {{1}}, ‘I do not know in which I am happier, the coming of Ja‘far or the conquest of Khaybar’: Sunan Abi Dawud; al-Hakim, al-Mustadrak; Ibn Hibban. The return to Madinah of Ja‘far (RA) from Abyssinia was in the seventh year of the Hijrah, at the time of the conquest of Khaybar. Many have called the narration hasan.

quiz.q: Why did some of the first emigrants return to Makkah?
o: A sudden famine struck Abyssinia
A false report that the Quraysh had softened
The Prophet ﷺ told them to return
Al-Najashi expelled them from the country
quiz.e: Coming near they found nothing had changed, rather it was harder than before; ‘Uthman ibn Maz‘un (RA) entered by taking protection.

quiz.q: What lesson does the return to Makkah on false news teach?
o: Making the hijrah was itself a mistake
Abyssinia was not really a safe place at all
The Prophet ﷺ had told them to come back
News to one’s liking is accepted without verification
quiz.e: What the heart wants to hear the ear takes as true; coming near they saw the news of relief was imagination.

quiz.q: What should be done on hearing news to one’s liking?
o: First verify it well
Believe at once
Spread it as fast as possible
Assume the exact opposite
quiz.e: What the heart wants the ear takes as true; part of the Companions returned without verifying and were deceived.

quiz.q: Who led the caravan of the second hijrah?
o: ‘Uthman ibn Maz‘un (RA)
al-Zubayr ibn al-‘Awwam (RA)
Ja‘far ibn Abi Talib (RA)
Abu Salamah ibn ‘Abd al-Asad (RA)
quiz.e: Cousin of the Prophet ﷺ, elder brother of ‘Ali (RA); he resembled the Prophet ﷺ in face and nature.

quiz.q: Who were the two envoys of the Quraysh in the court of al-Najashi?
o: Abu Jahl and Umayyah ibn Khalaf
‘Utbah and Shaybah, the two great warrior sons of Rabi‘ah
al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and al-‘As ibn Wa’il
‘Amr ibn al-‘As and ‘Abdullah ibn Abi Rabi‘ah
quiz.e: Two eloquent men; with them fine leather as gifts and bribes for the courtiers.

quiz.q: What did the envoys first do to win over al-Najashi?
o: Gave gifts to the monks and courtiers of the court
Secretly massed troops on the border
Wrote a false letter in the name of the Muslims
Gave a big bribe to the king’s son
quiz.e: First gifts were pressed into the hands of the courtiers, and through them the king’s ear was filled.

quiz.q: With what did Ja‘far (RA) begin his speech?
o: Long praise of King al-Najashi
‘We were an ignorant people’
A description of the Quraysh’s oppression
A detailed introduction of ‘Isa (AS)
quiz.e: No long preface; he laid out the picture of rising from ignorance to civilisation.

quiz.q: What was the structure of the speech of Ja‘far (RA)?
o: What we were, what he came and changed
Only long condemnation of the Quraysh
Standing only on legal and diplomatic argument
Long theological debate
quiz.e: No long preface; he drew the picture of rising from ignorance to civilisation.

quiz.q: At al-Najashi’s request, which surah did Ja‘far (RA) recite?
o: Surah Ya-Sin
Surah al-Rahman
Surah Maryam
Surah al-Fatihah
quiz.e: The beginning of Surah Maryam; the story of Maryam and ‘Isa (peace be upon them). The king and monks wept.

quiz.q: What does al-Najashi’s decision being overturned by one recitation show?
o: The king was actually weak-minded
True words reach the heart directly
The Quraysh envoys were incompetent at diplomacy
The monks of the court had plotted
quiz.e: Diplomacy, gifts, bribes; all were in the envoys’ hands. A few verses won.

quiz.q: On the second day, what did ‘Amr tell al-Najashi to ask the Muslims?
o: Why they left their country
Where exactly their Prophet had gone into hiding
What harm they had done the Quraysh
What they say about ‘Isa ibn Maryam
quiz.e: Whatever the answer, it was a trap; the Muslims decided, we will say what Allah has said.

quiz.q: Hearing the answer about ‘Isa (AS), what did al-Najashi do?
o: Picked up a twig and said ‘Isa was no more than this
Kept the Muslims in prison
Accepted all the gifts of the Quraysh
Summoned Ja‘far to an open debate before the courtiers
quiz.e: Ja‘far said, he is the servant of Allah and His Messenger, His spirit and His word; al-Najashi agreed and returned the gifts.

quiz.q: What is the significance of the Muslims’ decision in the trap of the second day?
o: They wanted to displease the king on purpose
They wanted to win the debate in court
Standing firm on the truth without calculating the consequence
They had not understood ‘Amr’s move
quiz.e: Whatever the answer, it was a trap; yet they told the truth, and that very truth saved them.

quiz.q: In a situation where one is caught in a trap, what to do according to the incident of the second day?
o: Save oneself by any means
Stay completely silent
Say the truth straight out
Turn the answer around cleverly
quiz.e: The Muslims said, we will say what Allah has said; and that very truth protected them.

quiz.q: What was the real name of al-Najashi?
o: Abrahah al-Ashram
al-Muqawqis al-Qibti
Ashamah
Heraclius Caesar
quiz.e: Najashi was a title; the real name was Ashamah. The Prophet ﷺ called him by this name at his absentee funeral prayer.

quiz.q: What did the Prophet ﷺ do on the day al-Najashi died?
o: Called a mourning gathering in Makkah
Led an absentee funeral prayer in Madinah
Sent a delegate to Abyssinia with condolences
Did nothing, nor even announced it
quiz.e: In Madinah he announced, today a righteous brother has died; Ashamah. At the praying ground he formed rows and prayed the funeral with four takbirs.

quiz.q: What is proved by the absentee funeral prayer for al-Najashi?
o: Absentee funeral prayer is sunnah for all the dead
Abyssinia had become a Muslim state
Four takbirs in the funeral prayer was then a new rule
Al-Najashi believed in the end
quiz.e: The Prophet ﷺ called him a ‘righteous brother’; justice and the weeping of one recitation had brought him to faith.

quiz.q: When did Ja‘far (RA) return from Abyssinia to Madinah?
o: At the time of Badr
At the time of Uhud
At the time of the conquest of Khaybar
At the time of the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah
quiz.e: The Prophet ﷺ said, I do not know in which I am happier; the conquest of Khaybar, or the coming of Ja‘far.

quiz.q: What is shown in the part ‘A Speech of One Sitting That Remained’?
o: Ordered true words work year after year
Ja‘far’s speech failed in the end
Ja‘far said a wrong thing in court that day
Al-Najashi later changed his decision
quiz.e: That speech of one sitting made Abyssinia a safe haven for many years.

quiz.q: When someone comes to argue about the din, what is useful at that moment?
o: Silencing him quickly
Showing anger at him
Having an ordered answer in hand
Avoiding the argument and moving away
quiz.e: Ordered true words spoken at the right time carry a word of one sitting very far; if not, the opportunity slips away.

quiz.q: What does the dars say about an environment where the child does not learn the din?
o: Changing environment is a kind of weakness
Moving is no shame, but after settling a safe destination
In this there is really nothing at all in our hands
Du‘a alone is enough
quiz.e: The Companions loved Makkah, yet by Allah’s command they moved; in the new place they held on to the din.

quiz.q: When does going to a good environment bring no benefit?
o: Going completely alone without family
Going very far away
Taking the inner habit along
Going secretly
quiz.e: Changing place helps only when a person takes the good inside himself and leaves the bad behind.

porbos.title: Now in Makkah: The Islam of Hamzah (RA) • Allah Sometimes Straightens Even Along a Crooked Path • The Day ‘Umar (RA) Went Out Sword in Hand • The Man Who Changed on a Single Page • After the Islam of ‘Umar • What a Single Page Can Do • Others Who Came • Final Word

blocks.0: Now in Makkah: The Islam of Hamzah (RA)
blocks.1: Leaving the news of Abyssinia here, let us return to Makkah. In Makkah the persecution was still going on. In the midst of it two events occurred that changed the whole reckoning. One day Abu Jahl found the Prophet {{1}} alone near the mount of Safa, said all sorts of things, and raised a hand against him. The Prophet {{2}} said not a word. He came away.
blocks.2: Nearby, a slave-woman of ‘Abdullah ibn Jud‘an stood and saw it all. That afternoon Hamzah (RA) returned from hunting, bow on his shoulder. He was one of the bravest men of Makkah, the uncle of the Prophet {{1}}, and his milk-brother.
blocks.3: The custom of Makkah was that on returning from hunting he would first circle the Ka‘bah. That day on the way the slave-woman stopped him and told him everything; how Abu Jahl had humiliated your nephew today, and he did not say a word.
blocks.4: Hamzah’s (RA) blood boiled. He went straight to the Ka‘bah, found Abu Jahl, and split his head with the bow. He said, you abuse my nephew! I too am on his din. If you can, settle it with me.{{1}}
blocks.5: Abu Jahl fell silent. When his men rose to their feet he stopped them; he said, leave it, I really did speak ill of his nephew. At first this was tribal stubbornness; why should anyone touch my man.
blocks.6: Allah Sometimes Straightens Even Along a Crooked Path
blocks.7: Hamzah (RA) came home. Back home a doubt struck him. I have said it with my mouth, I am on the din of Muhammad. But have I truly accepted it inside! Or did I say it in a fit of anger!
blocks.8: He remained restless all night. In the end he raised his hands to Allah, make my heart steady; let me stay on this path knowingly and understandingly. After that Allah opened his chest. The stubbornness took the form of faith.{{1}}
blocks.9: There is something to think about in this incident. The first step of Hamzah (RA) was not entirely with the right intention. Anger, tribal pride, the insult to the nephew; this was the pull. Yet the word that came out of the mouth from that anger was a true word. And Allah took hold of that truth and lifted him up.
blocks.10: We often tell ourselves, the intention is not right, so I do not even begin the deed. Yet often when the deed begins the intention is set right afterward. I began going to the mosque out of shame before people; later I went out of love. I took up the Qur’an for fear of the exam; later I found peace in the recitation itself.
blocks.11: When the intention is not right, a good deed should not be left aside. One holds on to the deed and mends the intention. Hamzah (RA), on returning home, did exactly this; he made du‘a and set his heart straight.
blocks.12: The Day ‘Umar (RA) Went Out Sword in Hand
blocks.13: This is a few days after the Islam of Hamzah (RA). ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab was then one of the fiercest enemies of Islam. A strong hand, a harsh temper, known as the envoy of Makkah.
blocks.14: One day he went out with a sword in hand. One intention only; today he would finish Muhammad. On the way he met Nu‘aym ibn ‘Abdillah; he had become a Muslim in secret. He asked, where are you going, ‘Umar. ‘Umar said, to Muhammad. To finish him.
blocks.15: Nu‘aym said, first set your own house in order. Your sister Fatimah and brother-in-law Sa‘id have taken that din. ‘Umar turned around. Now the target was his sister’s house. Nearing the house he heard someone inside reciting something in a low voice. Khabbab ibn al-Aratt (RA) was teaching them Surah Ta-Ha.
blocks.16: ‘Umar pushed the door and entered. He seized his brother-in-law Sa‘id and beat him. When his sister Fatimah tried to shield him, she was struck in the face too, and blood came out. With a blood-stained face Fatimah (RA) said, ‘Umar, do what you like. But we will not give up this din.{{1}}
blocks.17: His sister’s blood, and this word of his sister; the two together stopped ‘Umar. The anger inside him suddenly softened. He said, show me once what you were reading.
blocks.18: The Man Who Changed on a Single Page
blocks.19: Fatimah (RA) said, you are impure. Bathe before touching this writing. The hardest man of Makkah, hearing his sister’s word, bathed. Then he took the sheet in his hand.
blocks.20: On it was written the beginning of Surah Ta-Ha
blocks.22: Ta-Ha. I have not sent down this Qur’an to you that you should suffer. Rather it is an admonition for one who fears. It is a revelation from Him who created the earth and the lofty heavens. The Most Merciful is established above the Throne. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and whatever is between them, and whatever is beneath the soil.{{1}}
blocks.23: ‘Umar stopped as he read. He said, how beautiful is this word, how dignified. Khabbab (RA) had been hiding inside the house all this time. Coming out he said, ‘Umar, by Allah, I hope He has chosen you. Only yesterday I heard the Prophet {{1}} say, O Allah, strengthen Islam with ‘Umar or Abu Jahl.{{2}}
blocks.24: ‘Umar asked, where is Muhammad now. Khabbab (RA) said, near Safa, in Dar al-Arqam. ‘Umar went to Dar al-Arqam with that same sword in hand. He knocked at the door. The Companions were afraid; ‘Umar standing with a sword. Hamzah (RA) said, let him in. If he has come with a good intention, good; if with a bad intention, his matter will be settled with his own sword.
blocks.25: ‘Umar went inside and said, I bear witness that there is no deity but Allah, and you are the Messenger of Allah. Dar al-Arqam shook with the takbir. The people of Makkah heard that sound outside.
blocks.26: A man had left home to kill. After reading a single page of the Qur’an, he went back a Muslim.
blocks.28: ‘Umar (RA) was not one to accept Islam and stay quiet. He asked the Prophet {{1}}, are we not on the truth, whether we die or live! The Prophet {{2}} said, certainly. ‘Umar said, then why hide. Come, openly.
blocks.29: Until then the Companions did not dare to pray openly in front of the Ka‘bah. On the day of ‘Umar’s Islam that changed. That day the Companions went toward the Ka‘bah in two rows. At the head of one row Hamzah (RA), at the head of the other ‘Umar (RA).
blocks.30: The Quraysh stared, and could do nothing. That day the Muslims for the first time prayed openly, with open eyes, in front of the Ka‘bah. ‘Umar (RA) himself went and told the assembly of the Quraysh, I have become a Muslim. They flared up in anger, but no one had the courage to say anything to his face.
blocks.31: ‘Abdullah ibn Mas‘ud (RA) would say later, since the Islam of ‘Umar we have prayed with honour.{{1}}
blocks.32: One man’s inside changed. And on the strength of his courage the whole community stood with head raised. Sometimes one person’s firmness breaks the fear of a whole group. In a gathering, if one person dares to say the right thing, the others too find the strength to speak.
blocks.33: What a Single Page Can Do
blocks.34: What is the biggest point in the story of ‘Umar (RA)! Not the sword. Not the sister’s courage. Not even the Islam of Hamzah (RA). The biggest point: a man had set out to kill, and after reading one page of the Qur’an he went back a Muslim.
blocks.35: Within the Qur’an is a power that people do not want to open and see for themselves. ‘Umar had been told since childhood, this is poetry, this is magic, this is the raving of a madman. All this time without verifying himself he had believed those words. The moment he put his own eyes on it, all those notions fell apart on a single page.
blocks.36: We too hear many things and do not verify. The Qur’an is hard, I will not understand; reciting is enough, meaning is not needed; that is the work of scholars. We recite a lot. We pause little.
blocks.37: To stop before a verse and think, is this really being said to me; this is what stopped ‘Umar. The Qur’an that could change a man like ‘Umar in one sitting, that same Qur’an lies open before me every day.
blocks.38: The question is not about the power of the Qur’an. The question is whether I am sitting before it, pausing, with attention.
blocks.40: In this period a few more people came to Islam; each by a different path. Abu Dharr al-Ghifari (RA) had come earlier, stood before the Ka‘bah and testified openly and was beaten; that came in the last dars.{{1}}
blocks.41: Tufayl ibn ‘Amr al-Dawsi was a chief of a tribe and a well-known poet. Before he entered Makkah the Quraysh surrounded him; do not listen to Muhammad’s words, there is magic in his words; you and your tribe will be ruined.
blocks.42: He was so afraid that he went to the Ka‘bah with cotton stuffed in his ears, so that by mistake no word of the Prophet {{1}} would enter his ear. Yet a few words got into his ears. He thought, I am an intelligent man, a poet, I can tell good from bad. What is the use of cotton in my ears; let me listen once, if it is good I will take it, if bad I will leave it.
blocks.44: Dimad al-Azdi used to practise incantation-healing; treating jinn and wind. Coming to Makkah he heard people say Muhammad is mad. He thought, let me try, perhaps Allah will cure him at my hands.
blocks.45: Going to the Prophet {{1}} he said, let me hear your words once. The Prophet {{2}} spoke some words beginning with the praise of Allah. Dimad said, repeat these words to me. Then he said, I have heard the words of soothsayers, I have heard the words of sorcerers, I have heard the words of poets; such words I have heard from no one’s mouth. Take my pledge.{{3}}
blocks.46: Three people. They came in through three different doors. One from anger, one from curiosity, one with a wrong notion. One thing alone drew them all. Once the word had reached the ear, it could not be denied.
blocks.48: In today’s dars we saw what happened when persecution reached everyone. A group of Companions crossed the sea to Abyssinia to save the din. There the Qur’an reached a royal court, a Christian king wept, and in the end came as far as faith.
blocks.49: And in Makkah two men; Hamzah and ‘Umar (RA); came and stood by two different paths. Then the Muslims for the first time prayed with heads held high before the Ka‘bah. One thing came up again and again through the whole dars. One recitation overturned the king’s decision. One page of the Qur’an changed ‘Umar. A few words stopped Tufayl and Dimad.
blocks.50: That power of the Qur’an has not diminished even a little today. One more thing. Ja‘far (RA) did not give a long speech in the king’s court. He said two things; what we were before, and what he came and changed.
blocks.51: If someone suddenly asks today, what does your din actually teach; do I have an ordered answer like Ja‘far’s! Or do I glance about and turn the conversation?
blocks.52: So take one task from today’s dars. In your own words, in two or three lines, put in order an introduction to Islam. What people were like before, and what this din came and changed.
blocks.53: So that when someone asks you need not freeze. In the coming dars we shall see what the Quraysh did after these two accepted Islam; the whole of Banu Hashim was besieged in a valley for three years.
blocks.55: Ja‘far (RA), standing in the court of the emperor, said in two minutes what we were before and what this din came and changed. Today I will ask myself one question: if someone asks what my din teaches, will I be able to say it in order?
blocks.56: Today I will write a two-or-three-line introduction in my own words and memorise it, which from today I will no longer leave disordered.

footnotes.0: Concerning the humiliation of the Prophet {{1}} at the hands of Abu Jahl, the witness of the slave-woman of ‘Abdullah ibn Jud‘an, and Hamzah (RA) splitting Abu Jahl’s head with his bow and declaring Islam: Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham. The narration is of the Sirah works; the chain is mursal. That Hamzah (RA) accepted Islam in the earliest period and was later martyred at Uhud is established by sound chains.
footnotes.1: Concerning the doubt in the heart after Hamzah’s (RA) declaration of Islam, returning home, and gaining firmness by praying to Allah to steady the heart: Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham. The narration is of the Sirah works; the chain is mursal.
footnotes.2: Concerning ‘Umar (RA) going out sword in hand, meeting Nu‘aym, the sheet of Surah Ta-Ha in the house of his sister Fatimah and brother-in-law Sa‘id ibn Zayd (RA), and accepting Islam from there: Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham; al-Daraqutni; Ibn Sa‘d. The chain of the full incident is mursal and has some weakness. But the Islam of ‘Umar (RA) and its effect are established by sound chains.
footnotes.4: The du‘a of the Prophet {{1}}, ‘O Allah, strengthen Islam with ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab or Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, whichever of the two is dearer to You’, and ‘Umar’s (RA) acceptance of Islam the next day: Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi, hadith 3681; Musnad Ahmad; Ibn Majah, hadith 105. Many hadith scholars have called the narration hasan.
footnotes.5: ‘Ma zilna a‘izzatan mundhu aslama ‘Umar’; since ‘Umar’s Islam we have been honoured. Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 3684; via ‘Abdullah ibn Mas‘ud (RA). ✓ Verified. This is Ibn Mas‘ud’s (RA) own statement; sahih by the standard of Imam al-Bukhari.
footnotes.6: Details of the acceptance of Islam by Abu Dharr al-Ghifari (RA) and his open testimony of the kalimah in al-Masjid al-Haram: Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 3522; Sahih Muslim, hadith 2474. Given in detail in Dars 7.
footnotes.7: Concerning Tufayl ibn ‘Amr al-Dawsi (RA) going to the Ka‘bah with cotton in his ears and later accepting Islam: Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham. The narration is of the Sirah works; the chain is mursal.
footnotes.8: The incident of the acceptance of Islam by Dimad al-Azdi (RA): Sahih Muslim, hadith 868; via Ibn ‘Abbas (RA). ✓ Verified.

quiz.q: Who brought the news of Abu Jahl’s insult to Hamzah (RA)?
o: Abu Bakr (RA)
Khabbab ibn al-Aratt (RA)
The Prophet ﷺ himself told him
A slave-woman of ‘Abdullah ibn Jud‘an
quiz.e: The slave-woman had seen everything near the mount of Safa; she told Hamzah (RA), returning from the hunt.

quiz.q: With what did Hamzah (RA) split Abu Jahl’s head?
o: With a bow
With a sword
With a stone
With a staff
quiz.e: He had a bow on his shoulder returning from hunting; with it he went to the Ka‘bah and declared Islam.

quiz.q: What was the difference between Hamzah’s (RA) first step and his final faith?
o: Actually there was no difference between the two
First stubbornness, later steadiness of heart through du‘a
First firm faith, later doubt in the mind
First fear, later sudden courage
quiz.e: Back home a doubt struck him; he prayed to steady his heart, and the stubbornness took the form of faith.

quiz.q: What example does the dars give in support of ‘if the intention is not right, a deed should not be left’?
o: The martyrdom of Sumayyah bint Khayyat (RA)
Bilal’s (RA) word ‘Ahad’
Going to the mosque out of shame before people and later going out of love
The profitable deal of Suhayb (RA)
quiz.e: If one holds on to the deed the intention can be mended later; Hamzah (RA) did exactly this on returning home.

quiz.q: What is the advice about a good deed when the intention is not fully right?
o: Wait until the intention is right
Leave the deed aside for now
Do it only after informing people
Hold on to the deed and mend the intention
quiz.e: Going to the mosque began out of shame before people, later out of love; Hamzah (RA) prayed and straightened his heart.

quiz.q: Who turned ‘Umar (RA) toward his sister’s house?
o: Abu Jahl ibn Hisham
Nu‘aym ibn ‘Abdillah
Khabbab ibn al-Aratt (RA)
Hamzah ibn ‘Abd al-Muttalib (RA)
quiz.e: Nu‘aym told ‘Umar, who had set out sword in hand, first set your own house in order; your sister and brother-in-law have taken that din.

quiz.q: Who was teaching Surah Ta-Ha in ‘Umar’s sister’s house?
o: Mus‘ab ibn ‘Umayr (RA)
Bilal ibn Rabah (RA)
Khabbab ibn al-Aratt (RA)
al-Arqam ibn Abi al-Arqam (RA)
quiz.e: When ‘Umar entered, Khabbab (RA) hid; later he came out and spoke of the du‘a of the Prophet ﷺ.

quiz.q: What did Fatimah (RA) tell ‘Umar to do before touching the sheet?
o: Make wudu well first
Take off his shoes first
Put down the sword first
Bathe first
quiz.e: Saying you are impure she had him bathe first; then ‘Umar took the sheet in his hand.

quiz.q: Strengthening Islam through one of which two did the Prophet ﷺ pray for?
o: ‘Umar or Abu Jahl
Hamzah or ‘Abbas
Abu Bakr or ‘Uthman
‘Utbah or Shaybah
quiz.e: ‘O Allah, ‘Umar or Abu Jahl; strengthen Islam with the one dearer to You’; Tirmidhi 3681.

quiz.q: Who said to let ‘Umar in on seeing him with a sword in Dar al-Arqam?
o: Abu Bakr ibn Abi Quhafah (RA)
Hamzah (RA)
‘Ali ibn Abi Talib (RA)
Bilal ibn Rabah (RA)
quiz.e: Hamzah (RA) said, let him in; if with good intention, good, otherwise his matter will be settled with his own sword.

quiz.q: What were the Companions able to do for the first time after ‘Umar’s (RA) Islam?
o: Secretly send envoys to the tribes of Madinah
Make a written treaty with the Quraysh
Pray openly before the Ka‘bah
Migrate to Abyssinia in a group
quiz.e: In two rows, Hamzah and ‘Umar (RA) at the front; the Quraysh stared and could do nothing.

quiz.q: Who says, ‘since the Islam of ‘Umar we have prayed with honour’?
o: Abu Bakr ibn Abi Quhafah (RA)
Bilal ibn Rabah (RA)
Khabbab ibn al-Aratt (RA)
‘Abdullah ibn Mas‘ud (RA)
quiz.e: ‘Ma zilna a‘izzatan mundhu aslama ‘Umar’; Sahih al-Bukhari 3684, the statement of Ibn Mas‘ud (RA).

quiz.q: How does one person’s firmness change a whole group, from the story of ‘Umar?
o: By his becoming leader of the whole group
By his giving away his wealth
By his openly declaring war before everyone
Through his courage the rest gain strength to stand
quiz.e: ‘Umar, on accepting Islam, spoke of open prayer; from then the Companions prayed with heads raised.

quiz.q: In the story of ‘Umar’s Islam, what is the biggest point according to the dars?
o: The sword in his hand
The sister’s courage with a blood-stained face
Hamzah’s (RA) earlier acceptance of Islam
Changing on reading one page of the Qur’an
quiz.e: That power of the Qur’an which people do not want to open and see for themselves; ‘Umar changed because he paused and thought.

quiz.q: ‘The question is not about the power of the Qur’an, but whether I am sitting before it’; what does this mean?
o: To be affected, one must sit and pay attention
The Qur’an is really not for all people
Reciting more is enough
If one does not understand the meaning, recitation is of no benefit
quiz.e: We recite a lot, we pause little; one thought alone stopped ‘Umar.

quiz.q: Which habit does the dars name for benefiting from the Qur’an?
o: Pausing and thinking at one verse
Faster and more recitation
Only memorising well
Only reciting to others
quiz.e: ‘Is this being said to me?’; this thought is what stopped ‘Umar (RA).

quiz.q: What did Tufayl ibn ‘Amr do on going to the Ka‘bah out of fear of the Quraysh?
o: Blocked both ears with cotton
Covered his whole face with cloth
Kept both eyes closed the whole time
Took a few companions with him
quiz.e: The Quraysh had said there is magic in Muhammad’s words; yet when a few words got into his ears he decided to listen once.

quiz.q: What work did Dimad al-Azdi do?
o: Composed poetry
Practised incantation-healing
Traded in distant lands
Divined by watching the stars
quiz.e: Hearing ‘mad’ he went to cure him; hearing the words of the Prophet ﷺ he said, these are not the words of any madman. Sahih Muslim 868.

quiz.q: In the part ‘Others Who Came’, what is the common point in the Islam of the three?
o: All three were great tribal chiefs
Once the word reached the ear they could not deny it
All three were well-known poets
All three had been severely persecuted
quiz.e: One from anger, one from curiosity, one with a wrong notion; one thing alone drew them all.

quiz.q: What lesson does the part ‘Others Who Came’ give about da‘wah?
o: Getting the word to the ear is the real work
Everyone should be called in the same way
Only the intelligent should be called
Calling fierce opponents is utterly futile
quiz.e: Coming from anger, curiosity or a wrong notion they could not stay away; once the word reaches the ear denial is hard.

quiz.q: If someone asks ‘what does your din teach’, what is the preparation?
o: Send him to a scholar
Keep a two-or-three-line ordered introduction
Hand him a long book
Cleverly avoid the question somehow
quiz.e: Ja‘far said in two minutes what we were before and what he came and changed; today’s practical resolve is this too.

quiz.q: What is the practical resolve of this dars?
o: Keep an ordered introduction to the din in one’s own words
Recite one juz a day
Read a large book of the Sirah
Invite at least one person a week
quiz.e: What people were like before, and what this din came and changed; so that when someone asks one need not freeze.
